title: He should have left them.
paragraphs: He should have left them.
That’s what our flesh expects after reading Nehemiah 9.

Israel rebels.
God rescues.
Israel forgets.
God warns.
Israel falls.
God forgives.

Again.
And again.
And again.

Nehemiah 9 is not just Israel’s history.
It is a mirror.

They made idols after seeing miracles.
They hardened their necks after tasting mercy.
They traded the glory of God for the madness of their own desires.
And still Scripture says He is “a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (Nehemiah 9:17).
Pause there.
Ready to forgive.

Not irritated to forgive.
Not reluctant to forgive.
Not cornered into forgiveness.
Ready.
But here’s what we miss: God’s repeated forgiveness does not make sin small. It makes grace look massive.

Israel’s story is the story of every human heart.
We wander.
We forget.
We love gifts more than the Giver.
We promise loyalty, then chase idols with the same hands we lifted in worship.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Nehemiah 9 does not glorify Israel’s failure.
It glorifies God’s covenant mercy.

He fed them in the wilderness.
He guided them by cloud and fire.
He did not abandon them in their rebellion.
Even when they were faithless, He remained righteous.
That mercy points forward to Jesus.

Because the deepest answer to Israel’s repeated failure is not better human effort.
It is the cross.

At Calvary, the God who is “ready to forgive” made a way to forgive justly.
Jesus bore the judgment rebels deserve so rebels could be welcomed home.
Not excused.
Redeemed.

So if you feel ashamed by how many times you’ve failed God, read Nehemiah 9 again.
Then look to Christ.

Your sin may be repeated.
But His mercy is not exhausted.

Repent.
Return.
Run back to Jesus.
Nehemiah 9:17, 19, 31
